Lessons.Title: Completing the Square (Part 1)
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: convert a monic quadratic equation to an equivalent perfect-square equation by adding (b/2)² to both sides, and then solve using positive/negative square roots. Independently authored Edulytiks adaptation of Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 7 Lesson 12 teacher https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/7/12/preparation.html and student https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/students/1/7/12/index.html (CC BY 4.0). This source introduces the method using integer-friendly coefficients.
Original equation x²+8x=9. Half coefficient8 is4; square is16. Add16 to BOTH sides: x²+8x+16=25, or (x+4)²=25. Thus x+4=±5 and x=1 or−9. Direct substitution gives at1 1+8=9; at−9 81−72=9.

A second example x²−6x=7 requires adding9, yielding (x−3)²=16, giving x7 or−1. The completed-square constant depends on half the linear coefficient, including its sign, but squared constant itself is nonnegative. The method preserves equivalence only when the same addition is applied to both sides.

Student task: complete two monic squares, explain geometrically the missing corner needed to make a square, critique a step adding16 only on left, and check both roots. Teacher-scored rubric0–2 for the added term, legitimate equation transformation, full root set and verification.

KeyConcepts.Title: Completing term
KeyConcepts.Definition: For x²+bx, add (b/2)² to form a perfect square.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equation equivalence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adding same number to both sides preserves solutions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Add16 to both sides of x²+8x=9.
